newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Ford British job deal averts strike.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Ford British job deal averts strike.

text.p: U.S. car giant Ford Motor Co on Friday averted the threat of a national strike by British workers by clinching a deal with trade unions to secure the future of its Halewood plant in northwest England.
Ford, which had threatened to slash 1,300 jobs at the plant in north east England, said after two days of talks with unions that it would now only cut 980.
The company also said it had committed itself to additional investment in Britain which could amount to "hundreds of millions of pounds."

Jac Nasser, head of Ford's European division, hailed the deal as a "fair agreement that takes into account what is good for Britain, the workforce and what is good for Ford." Roger Butler, of the Amalgamated Engineers and Electricians Unions (AEEU), called it "a major victory for Ford workers."

Ford said the new investment was planned for its Southampton plant where the new Ford Transit model would be built. There will also be a Transit-related investment for metal stamping at its Dagenham plant and transmissions components in Halewood.

Another large investment is planned at Dagenham in Essex which has been chosen as the long-term strategic source for the Ford Fiesta model. It will also be the lead plant for the next version of the Fiesta, Ford said.

The deal followed two days of talks between Nasser and union leaders in a last ditch effort by the workers to try to save 1,300 jobs set to go after Ford's decision last month to move production of its new Escort model to Continental Europe.
Production of the Escort would switch to Germany and Spain.
A threat of a strike by all Ford workers in Britain was called off after the deal, which is expected to be put to a meeting of Halewood workers next week.

Failure of the talks would have resulted in unions calling a strike ballot next week which could have led up to 20,000 Ford production line workers going on strike just ahead of a British election, which must be called by May 22.
Earlier one union official outlined the points put forward to the Ford management in the talks.

"Our arguments are that there is no economic reason for this. The plant has increased productivity, labour costs are down and we have met all our targets. The only reason for moving the jobs to the continent is that the cost of sacking people in Britain is cheaper."
Unions have claimed it is less expensive to cut jobs in Britain because the government has opted out of the European Union's Social Chapter which gives greater protection to employees.

Industry analyst LMC International says the move to cut jobs was triggered by heavy losses in Ford's European arm due to sluggish regional demand, particularly in the French and German markets which make up about 40 percent of Ford's European sales.
The U.S. car giant has also been trying to negotiate an increased subsidy from the British government to secure the future of the plant.

Both unions and Ford remained locked in talks with the government to try to secure a state subsidy to assist Halewood. Ford bosses said this would be a possible factor in deciding whether to build a new people carrier vehicle at the plant.
